knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", echo = FALSE)

This notebook records checks on the method as they are done. Results are
written down as observed at the time and are **not** recomputed when the
page is rebuilt. Later findings are added as new dated entries (or dated
notes) rather than by editing earlier results.

Each entry links to the script that reproduces it, in `dev/checks/`. Run
scripts from the package root. Outputs go to `$SURVIVER_CHECKS_OUT`
(default: a temporary folder).

## Status and open questions

*Last updated 2026-11-25.*

| Question | Status | Entry |
|---|---|---|
| Does `fit_ve()` recover a known VE(t)? | Yes, broadly; 92–93% of days inside the 90% CrI | [#1](#e01) |
| Why is the estimated curve about a week behind the truth? | Reporting time vs infection time. **Deferred** to the planned delay extension | [#1](#e01) |
| Why is late (90+ day) VE underestimated in the waning scenario? | About half explained by calendar time leaking into time since vaccination. Remainder within noise | [#2](#e02), [#3](#e03) |
| Do unreported (immune) infections in the risk set bias VE? | No detectable effect | [#2](#e02) |
| Does the FoI offset improve precision? | Not in this simulation once calendar time is adjusted for | [#3](#e03) |
| Is the remaining late bias real or chance? | **Open**: needs replicate simulations | — |
| Is a frailty term needed? | **Open**: decide after replicate simulations | — |

### Next steps

1. Let transmission vary over calendar time in the Stan model (e.g. a random
   walk on `log_beta` by day or week), keeping the FoI offset.
2. Run 20–50 replicate HERMES simulations per scenario to measure bias and
   interval coverage, rather than judging from one realisation.
3. Revisit frailty once (1) and (2) are done.

## 2026-11-25 — #1: Recovery of VE(t) on simulated data {#e01}

**Question.** Does `fit_ve()` (non-centred random-walk model, default
settings) recover the true VE(t) in the two HERMES scenarios, and can it tell
waning from no waning?

**Data.** `ve_sim_waning` and `ve_sim_no_waning` (10,000 people, 180 days,
16 vaccination rounds; HERMES commit `6c9ab73`). True VE ramps linearly from
0 to 0.8 over 14 days, then either decays (half-life 45 days, floor 0.1) or
stays at 0.8.

**Method.** Full population, age-structured FoI from `polymod_nl` with
`theta = 0`, infectious period 7 days starting 2 days before reporting, lag 1
day. Every day since vaccination gets its own bin (160 bins). 4 chains,
1,000 warm-up + 1,000 sampling iterations, `adapt_delta = 0.95`, seed 42.

**Script.** `dev/checks/2026-11-25_01_recovery.R` (about 1–2 minutes).

**Results.**

- Converged in both scenarios: max R-hat 1.004, min bulk ESS about 3,900,
  1 divergent transition in 4,000 (waning) and none (no waning). 30–45 s per
  fit.
- `log_beta` −4.51 (waning), −4.48 (no waning). `sigma_gamma` 0.12 and 0.18.
- True VE inside the 90% CrI on 93% (waning) and 92% (no waning) of days.

Average VE over each range of days since vaccination (true VE is averaged over
the same days; e.g. 0.20 for days 1–6 is the mean of the ramp 0.06…0.34):

| Days since vaccination | Waning: true | Waning: estimate (90% CrI) | No waning: true | No waning: estimate (90% CrI) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1–6 | 0.20 | 0.22 (−0.12, 0.45) | 0.20 | 0.11 (−0.31, 0.40) |
| 7–13 | 0.57 | 0.32 (0.05, 0.51) | 0.57 | 0.27 (−0.06, 0.49) |
| 14–29 | 0.73 | 0.61 (0.45, 0.74) | 0.80 | 0.64 (0.45, 0.78) |
| 30–44 | 0.59 | 0.68 (0.54, 0.80) | 0.80 | 0.74 (0.58, 0.84) |
| 45–59 | 0.49 | 0.57 (0.38, 0.71) | 0.80 | 0.74 (0.58, 0.85) |
| 60–89 | 0.38 | 0.43 (0.16, 0.62) | 0.80 | 0.82 (0.67, 0.91) |
| 90+ | 0.23 | 0.01 (−0.70, 0.44) | 0.80 | 0.84 (0.47, 0.96) |

```{r, fig.alt = "Estimated VE by day since vaccination with 90% credible band, against the true curve, for the waning and no-waning scenarios."}
fig("2026-11-25_01_recovery.png")
```

**Observations.**

1. The two scenarios are clearly distinguished: a rise then decline in the
   waning scenario, a plateau near 0.8 in the no-waning scenario.
2. The estimate lags the truth by about a week. Shifting the true curve
   right minimises the mean absolute error (days 1–120) at 6 days (waning)
   and 7–8 days (no waning).
   "Days since vaccination" is measured to the reporting day, while
   protection acts at infection, roughly 5 days (incubation) plus 2 days
   (reporting delay) earlier.
3. In the waning scenario the estimate falls below the truth after about
   day 90 (to around 0 against a true 0.2), with wide intervals that still
   contain the truth.

**Conclusion.** The method works on this data. The lag is expected and will
be handled by the planned extension for delays. The late underestimate needs
explaining (entries #2 and #3).

## 2026-11-25 — #2: Do unreported infections in the risk set cause the late drop? {#e02}

**Question.** About 28% of HERMES infections are never reported (20%
asymptomatic, plus 10% of symptomatic cases missed). These people are immune
but stay "at risk" in the data, mostly in the unvaccinated group. Does this
explain the late underestimate in #1?

**Method.** Regenerate both scenarios with HERMES to recover every person's
true `time_of_infection` (the regenerated runs were checked to be identical
to the packaged data). Refit the #1 model twice per scenario:

- **reported only**: as in #1;
- **true risk set**: people infected but never reported are censored at their
  true infection time.

Events (reported cases at their report day), FoI and all settings are
unchanged, so any difference is due only to the unreported infections.

**Script.** `dev/checks/2026-11-25_02_true_risk_set.R` (needs a local
`ibm_hermes` clone; about 2–3 minutes).

**Results.**

- Unreported infections censored: 627 (waning; 570 unvaccinated and 57
  vaccinated at infection) and 623 (no waning; 596 and 27).
- Estimates are essentially unchanged:

| Days since vaccination | True VE | Reported only | True risk set |
|---|---|---|---|
| 14–29 | 0.73 | 0.61 | 0.61 |
| 30–44 | 0.59 | 0.68 | 0.68 |
| 60–89 | 0.38 | 0.43 | 0.43 |
| 90–119 | 0.28 | 0.13 | 0.14 |
| 120+ | 0.20 | −0.08 | −0.07 |

*(waning scenario; averages over each range of days)*

- Mean error from day 90 on (estimate − truth): −0.22 vs −0.21 (waning);
  +0.04 vs +0.05 (no waning). Coverage 92–93% in all four fits.

```{r, fig.alt = "Estimated VE with the reported-only and true risk sets overlaid; the two curves are nearly identical in both scenarios."}
fig("2026-11-25_02_true_risk_set.png")
```

**Conclusion.** Unreported infections are not the cause. Removing about 600
people (roughly 10% of the remaining unvaccinated, leaving gradually) barely
changes the unvaccinated person-time, and the overall level is absorbed by
`log_beta`. A correction for unreported infections is not a priority for
VE(t).

---

## 2026-11-25 — #3: Is calendar time leaking into time since vaccination? {#e03}

**Question.** Long times since vaccination are only observed late in the
epidemic (you must have been vaccinated early). The model has one
transmission level for the whole study and relies on the FoI offset to track
calendar time. If the FoI fits poorly late in the epidemic, the leftover
error lands on the late time-since-vaccination bins. Does adjusting for
calendar day remove the late drop?

**Method.** Frequentist Poisson GLMs on the same cells as the Stan model,
with one VE per range of days since vaccination (piecewise constant):

- **A**: one baseline + FoI offset (the Stan model's structure);
- **B**: a separate baseline for each calendar day + FoI offset;
- **C**: a separate baseline for each calendar day + age group, no FoI
  (equivalent to a Cox model on calendar time).

Days with no cases at all are dropped for B and C, since they carry no
information once each day has its own baseline. The true VE per range is the
mean over vaccinated person-days.

**Script.** `dev/checks/2026-11-25_03_calendar_time.R` (seconds; base R).

**Results** (waning scenario, VE with 90% CI):

| Days since vaccination | Cases (vaccinated) | True VE | A | B | C |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1–6 | 23 | 0.20 | 0.09 (−0.29, 0.35) | 0.08 (−0.30, 0.35) | 0.07 (−0.31, 0.35) |
| 7–13 | 24 | 0.57 | 0.18 (−0.15, 0.42) | 0.19 (−0.14, 0.42) | 0.18 (−0.15, 0.42) |
| 14–29 | 21 | 0.73 | 0.68 (0.55, 0.78) | 0.69 (0.55, 0.78) | 0.68 (0.55, 0.78) |
| 30–44 | 15 | 0.59 | 0.73 (0.58, 0.82) | 0.74 (0.60, 0.83) | 0.74 (0.60, 0.83) |
| 45–59 | 22 | 0.49 | 0.53 (0.32, 0.67) | 0.55 (0.36, 0.68) | 0.55 (0.36, 0.68) |
| 60–89 | 36 | 0.38 | 0.42 (0.24, 0.56) | 0.47 (0.30, 0.60) | 0.47 (0.30, 0.60) |
| 90–119 | 28 | 0.28 | 0.10 (−0.23, 0.35) | 0.21 (−0.09, 0.43) | 0.22 (−0.08, 0.44) |
| 120+ | 13 | 0.21 | −0.11 (−0.76, 0.30) | 0.05 (−0.53, 0.41) | 0.07 (−0.50, 0.43) |

Case-weighted mean error from day 90 on: **A −0.22, B −0.10, C −0.08**
(waning); A 0.00, B +0.03, C +0.04 (no waning, where there are only 3
vaccinated cases at 90–119 days and none at 120+, so 120+ is not estimable).

```{r, fig.alt = "Point estimates and 90% intervals by range of days since vaccination for models A, B and C, with the true VE marked; B and C sit closer to the truth than A from day 90 on."}
fig("2026-11-25_03_calendar_time.png")
```

**Observations.**

1. Model A reproduces the Stan model's late error (−0.22), so the
   piecewise GLM is a fair stand-in for this question.
2. A per-day baseline roughly halves the late error. Earlier ranges barely
   change.
3. The remaining error (about −0.1) is well inside the intervals (41
   vaccinated cases after day 90); one realisation cannot separate it from
   chance.
4. B and C give almost identical estimates and interval widths: once each day
   has its own baseline, the POLYMOD-based FoI adds nothing beyond an age
   effect here. This may reflect that POLYMOD contacts do not describe how
   HERMES transmits (households, schools, workplaces). Relevant to the
   project's premise that FoI improves precision; worth revisiting with a
   FoI built from the simulation's own contact structure.

**Conclusion.** Calendar-time confounding explains about half of the late
underestimate. Next: add calendar-time flexibility to the Stan model, then
judge any remaining bias, and the need for frailty, with replicate
simulations.
